title: He Died Eight Days Before the Society He Helped Build Held Its First Show
standfirst: Périclès Pantazis died in Brussels on 25 January 1884, and Les XX — the group that would remake Belgian art for a decade — opened its first exhibition eight days later with his paintings on the walls. What's actually documented about this canvas, painted a few years earlier, turns out to be far thinner than his reputation.

sections.heading: The File Behind This Painting Calls It Impressionism. WikiArt Calls It Realism.
sections.body: The record this feature draws from tags this canvas "Impressionism." [WikiArt's own listing](https://www.wikiart.org/en/pericles-pantazis/dutch-girl-1880) tags the same painting "Realism," filed under portraiture. Both labels have a real claim on the man who painted it. In Paris, Pantazis trained under Gustave Courbet and Antoine Chintreuil — Courbet being Realism's own founding polemicist — before a reference letter from Manet carried him into Brussels and introduced him to Boudin, Jongkind, Pissarro and Degas. He carried both lineages into a city that hadn't settled the question either: by 1883 he belonged to the anti-academic [circle known as La Patte de Dindon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A9ricl%C3%A8s_Pantazis), and was among the painters invited to bring the newly formed Les XX up to its full twenty members. A hand trained by a Realist and vouched for by an Impressionist does not sort itself into a single field just because a database needs one.

sections.heading: Even the Painting's Own Title Is Nearly the Only Fact That Survives
sections.body: Beyond the title and the year, almost nothing about this specific canvas is recorded. WikiArt lists no sitter, no commission and no exhibition history for it — only a date, 1880, and a genre, portrait, on [the painting's own page](https://www.wikiart.org/en/pericles-pantazis/dutch-girl-1880). That thinness fits the period: after Pantazis settled back in Brussels in 1881, the paper trail around his last three years grows noticeably sparser, and what survives comes mostly through museum catalogues rather than his own letters. A Greek painter working in Belgium giving a Dutch title to an unnamed sitter is, on the evidence available, simply what happened. Nothing further has turned up to explain it, and inventing a reason would be worse than leaving the question open.

sections.heading: He Was Hired to Paint Walls, and Ended Up Teaching the House Painter
sections.body: [Guillaume Vogels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillaume_Vogels) ran a house-painting and decorating firm in Brussels, and for about a year Pantazis worked for him applying paint to walls rather than canvas. The instruction ran backwards from what that arrangement implied. Pantazis is credited with introducing his employer to the example of Courbet and Manet and teaching him to work with a palette knife, a technique Vogels carried into the loose, undated landscapes that later made his own reputation and that critics would eventually read as anticipating Expressionism. Vogels outlived the man who taught him by twelve years, joined Les XX himself the year after Pantazis died, and went on study tours to England and the Netherlands with James Ensor — trips the painter who'd handed him the palette knife never got to take.

sections.heading: He Represented Greece at a Paris Fair He'd Already Left Behind
sections.body: A Greek wine merchant named Jean Économou became one of Pantazis's steadiest Brussels patrons, commissioning enough work that his name recurs through the painter's exhibition history. In 1878 Pantazis represented Greece at the Exposition Universelle in Paris — a country he had left as a student years before. He returned there properly only in 1880, travelling south through France and on to an [exhibition in Athens](https://www.nationalgallery.gr/en/artist/pantazis-periklis/) the following year, before going back to Brussels in 1881. It was after that return that tuberculosis symptoms appeared, the illness that killed him within three years. His market, his friendships and the professional circles that shaped his final decade were Belgian throughout; the flag he exhibited under in Paris was, by 1878, mostly attached to a passport.

sections.heading: The Group He Helped Build Opened Its Doors Eight Days After He Died
sections.body: Sources disagree about what to call his role in what came next. [The Odon Wagner Gallery's account](https://odonwagnergallery.com/artist/pericles-pantazis/biography/) states plainly that Pantazis "founded Les Vingt." Wikipedia's own entry on the group tells a narrower story: eleven artists founded [Les XX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_XX) on 28 October 1883, unhappy with the official Salon and with the internal politics of an older circle called L'Essor, and Pantazis was among nine further painters invited afterward to bring the society up to its full complement of twenty. Whichever version is right, he did not get to see it work. He died in Brussels on 25 January 1884. Les XX opened its first exhibition at the Palais des Beaux-Arts eight days later, on 2 February, with his paintings hung among the rest — the only appearance he ever made at a society built to run for a decade and reshape what got shown in Belgium.

sections.heading: Twenty-One Years After He Died, His Paintings Were Still on Belgian Walls
sections.body: The only major monograph on Pantazis, published by the [Averoff Museum](https://www.averoffmuseum.gr/en/ekdoseis/pericles-pantazis-1849-1884) in 1995, carries an essay by the art historian Stefanos Samaras titled "Pericles Pantazis: A destiny that was not fulfilled." It's a fair description of a career cut off at thirty-four, mid-argument, before its own society had held a single show. But the record suggests the argument kept landing without him: sixteen of his works sit in the [National Gallery in Athens](https://www.nationalgallery.gr/en/artist/pantazis-periklis/), more hang in museums in Antwerp, Brussels, Oostende and Sint-Niklaas, and a [database of early-twentieth-century exhibitions](https://exhibitions.univie.ac.at/person/ulan/500426137) records three of his paintings still being shown at La Libre Esthétique — the society Les XX became — in February 1905, twenty-one years after he died. An unfulfilled destiny doesn't usually keep getting invited back.
